trace.goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: The answer should present Informatica as a long-duration enterprise software story rather than a quick-win startup story.
It should mention the multiple liquidity events or strategic resets across decades.
It should turn the timeline into a lesson about endurance, reinvention, or strategic value in enterprise software.
rubric_must_haves: Explains why the long arc matters to founders.
Connects the acquisition to broader SaaS or AI infrastructure lessons.
Avoids empty nostalgia and extracts an operator takeaway.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer frames Informatica as proof that major enterprise outcomes often take decades, multiple market cycles, and repeated reinvention. The lesson should be that enterprise value compounds when a company becomes critical infrastructure, and that founders often underestimate how long durable category leadership can take to build.
trace.prompt:
Write a blog post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: The Wild Ride of Informatica: 32 Years, 2 IPOs, to $8 Billion Acquisition by Salesforce

Style examples from train-owned source text.
Use them for voice only. They are not evidence for claims.
Do not copy long passages verbatim.
[Style 1]
Dear SaaStr: How Can You Ensure a Smooth Transition When A New Team Member Takes Over a Customer Account?
Add value in the first interaction.  This is so rare.
There’s nothing more frustrating than getting a random email, “Hi, Tony is gone from the company. I know nothing about you, but I’m your new rep. Can we schedule a call?”
Find some way to add value.
One great way is to demo upcoming features / an upcoming release.
“Hi, I’m Jason, your next account exec. I’d love to find a way to help even more. Can I show you or anyone on your team the new AI features we’re launching shortly? There’s no additional cost for them and based on what I can see, they may radically increase your efficiency.”
Not perfect. But much better.
A second, albeit riskier, way to add value is to set up a call asking for “honest feedback on how we’re doing.”
This works, too.  Customers often just want to be heard.  The “problem” is you might have to do something about it.
[Style 2]
Dear SaaStr: When Is It Too Soon to Target Enterprise Customers in SaaS?
It too soon to target enterprise clients when you can’t support their needs 90 days
after
you close them.
It’s sort of OK in the enterprise to promise features and functionality that are sort of there … so long as you deliver them fairly promptly after the deal closes.
In fact, it happens all the time. Enterprise customers will even sign contracts agreeing to buy so long as you implement a key feature with X number of days.
But if you don’t have the team, commitment and experience to deliver that functionality at least X days after you close a Big Customer … you aren’t ready.  They’ll churn or at least, never fully deploy.
You don’t have to have the full enterprise package in the early days to close enterprise customers, especially if they have interest in you.  You’ll get some slack as a new, emerging vendor.  Especially if you have a strong deployment team.
But you have to meet your commitments and promises to them fairly soon after the deal closes.

trace.answer:
The Bumpy Road to Success: Informatica’s Epic Journey From Data Integration to Cloud Dominance
For over three decades, Informatica has been quietly building one of the most remarkable success stories in enterprise software history – a true case study in resilience, reinvention, and market timing.
Founded in 1988 by Gaurav Dhillon and Daniel Biesiadecki in Menlo Park, California, this data management powerhouse has undergone transformations few companies survive let alone thrive through. Through two IPOs, massive valuation swings, strategic acquisitions, and navigating the treacherous landscape of tech industry consolidation, Informatics has emerged stronger than ever.
Their latest chapter begins with an extraordinary announcement: they’ve agreed to sell to Salesforce for approximately $8 billion—marking another major milestone in their journey toward becoming a cloud-native enterprise software giant. Let’s take a deep dive into the fascinating story behind Informatica’s rise to become one of Silicon Valley’s most enduring successes.
The Early Days: Building Foundations
Informatica started with a simple yet powerful vision—to make complex data integration accessible to businesses of all sizes. In the late 1980s, when data warehousing was still in its infancy, these Stanford University graduates identified an enormous gap between business intelligence aspirations and technical reality. Their pioneering work helped lay the groundwork for modern big data analytics.

retrieval_hits.text:
1. Salesforce: +9,296% (Marc Benioff – Founder)
IPO Date:
June 2004 |
Split-Adjusted IPO Price:
$2.75 |
Current:
$258
The numbers are so staggering they require a double-take. After accounting for Salesforce’s 4-for-1 stock split in 2013, Marc Benioff’s cloud computing revolution delivered returns that approach 100x.
Benioff didn’t just create a company—he created an entire industry. When Salesforce went public in 2004, cloud software was still a radical concept. His vision of “No Software” seemed almost absurd to enterprise buyers accustomed to on-premise installations.
What Made It Legendary:
Category Creation:
Literally invented cloud software for enterprises
Platform Vision:
Built the AppExchange ecosystem that became a $4B+ marketplace
Relentless Innovation:
Never stopped evolving from CRM to AI to complete customer platform
20-Year Execution:
Sustained hypergrowth for two decades as a public company
$10,000 invested at IPO would be worth $939,636 today.

So Salesforce has now grown into the active granddad of SaaS.  Maybe not growing quite as fast as it once did.  But it’s matured into a true force of nature.  Only Microsoft, Oracle and now Salesforce have crossed $40 Billion in enterprise software ARR:
$40 Billion in ARR
Growing 9%
33% Non-GAAP Operating Margins (19% GAAP)
Generating $13B of free cash flow a year!!
Perhaps most importantly, Salesforce has leaned deeply into AI … and while the early usage is impressive, so far it hasn’t materially changed growth.  So far:
Since October, closed 5,000 Agentforce deals, including more than 3,000 paid just 90 days after officially launching
Salesforce says
Agentforce has managed 380,000 conversations
, with only 2% escalated to humans and an 84% resolution rate
So far, at the public company level, it’s the infra players that are seeing the crazy AI growth.  Nvidia, Google Cloud, Azure, etc.  But how about 2026+?  We’ll see.  As Marc Benioff notes below, Salesforce’s just started.  It’s only been selling AgentForce for a few months.  He’s incredibly excited and bullish on where it’s going.  It’s rejuvenated him.  Maybe AI will for all of us.

FY25 $37.9B
FY24 $34.9B
FY23 $31.4B
FY22 $26.5B
Salesforce Operating Cash Flow:
FY26 $14.5B (guidance)
FY25 $13.1B

FY22 $6.0B
Salesforce Margin:
FY26 34% (guidance)
FY25 33%
FY24 30.5%
FY23 22.5%
FY22 18.7%…

I remember when I made the first VC pitch deck for EchoSign in late 2005

Salesforce was worth a cool $2 Billion

(So I said maybe we could get 40% of the way there, an $800m exit, if all went perfectly)

19 years later, Salesforce is worth $300 Billion

Salesforce is the largest SaaS company, and soon, will be the largest biggest software company of all, passing SAP.  It’s already passed Oracle.
And as much, it’s really a bellwether of SaaS and Cloud.

in SaaS and Cloud.  Even
more so
after Covid.
